symbols.name: n
symbols.def: The number of independently sampled observational units.

symbols.name: d
symbols.def: The fixed dimension of the covariate vector.

symbols.name: a
symbols.def: The treatment level indexing potential outcomes and regressions.

symbols.name: u
symbols.def: A generic H\"older smoothness order.

symbols.name: m_u
symbols.type: strict integer part of the smoothness order
symbols.def: \(m_u=\lceil u\rceil-1\), the largest nonnegative integer strictly smaller than \(u\).

symbols.name: \alpha
symbols.def: The H\"older order of the propensity score.

symbols.name: \beta
symbols.def: The H\"older order of the treatment-specific outcome regressions.

symbols.name: \gamma
symbols.def: The H\"older order of the CATE.

symbols.name: s
symbols.def: \(s=(\alpha+\beta)/2\).

symbols.name: L
symbols.def: A fixed envelope for H\"older norms and bounded outcomes.

symbols.name: \varepsilon
symbols.def: The fixed lower bound on both treatment probabilities.

symbols.name: f_{-}
symbols.def: The fixed positive lower envelope for the covariate density.

symbols.name: f_{+}
symbols.def: The fixed upper envelope for the covariate density.

symbols.name: x_0
symbols.def: A fixed interior covariate value at which the CATE is evaluated.

symbols.name: Y(0)
symbols.def: The potential outcome under control.

symbols.name: Y(1)
symbols.def: The potential outcome under treatment.

symbols.name: A
symbols.def: The observed binary treatment.

symbols.name: X
symbols.def: The observed pre-treatment covariate vector.

symbols.name: Y
symbols.def: The realized outcome.

symbols.name: P
symbols.def: A law for the potential outcomes and the observed data.

symbols.name: f_P
symbols.def: The Lebesgue density of \(X\) under \(P\).

symbols.name: \pi_P
symbols.def: \(\pi_P(x)=P(A=1\mid X=x)\).

symbols.name: \mu_{a,P}
symbols.def: \(\mu_{a,P}(x)=\mathbb{E}_P[Y\mid A=a,X=x]\).

symbols.name: \mathcal{H}^{u}_d(L)
symbols.def: The radius-\(L\) isotropic H\"older ball of order \(u\), constructed in \(\mathrm{def:holder-ball}\).

symbols.name: \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{low}}
symbols.def: The strict smoothness region constructed in \(\mathrm{def:low-smoothness-region}\).

symbols.name: \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{band},n}
symbols.space: sets of full-data laws indexed by \(n\)
symbols.def: The primitive causal law class constructed in \(\mathrm{def:band-class}\).

symbols.name: R_n^{\mathrm{band}}
symbols.def: The pointwise CATE minimax risk constructed in \(\mathrm{def:band-risk}\).

symbols.name: r_n^{\mathrm{KBRW}}
symbols.def: The published density-qualified pointwise CATE benchmark constructed in \(\mathrm{def:kbrw-rate}\).

symbols.name: r_n^{\mathrm{band}}
symbols.def: The candidate polynomial minimax rate constructed in \(\mathrm{def:band-rate}\).

symbols.name: \overline r_n^{\mathrm{band}}
symbols.def: The logarithmically inflated upper rate constructed in \(\mathrm{def:band-upper-rate}\).

symbols.name: k_n
symbols.def: \(k_n=\lfloor n/(\log n)^2\rfloor\).

symbols.name: \widehat{\tau}^{\mathrm{cap}}_n(x_0)
symbols.space: measurable functions of \(O_{1:n}\) with values in \(\mathbb{R}\)
symbols.def: The cross-fitted estimator constructed in \(\mathrm{def:rank-capped-estimator}\).

symbols.name: \mathfrak{H}^{\mathrm{dens}}_n
symbols.def: The joint density, propensity, and regression perturbation program constructed in \(\mathrm{def:density-coupled-handle}\).

symbols.name: \mathfrak{H}^{\mathrm{asym}}
symbols.space: estimator and testing programs over band-only CATE experiments
symbols.def: The route for the unresolved exact frontier constructed in \(\mathrm{def:asymmetric-frontier-handle}\).

definitions.name: \mathcal{H}^{u}_d(L)
definitions.construction: \[\mathcal{H}^{u}_d(L)=\left\{g:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb{R}:\max_{|v|\le m_u}\lVert D^v g\rVert_\infty\le L,\ \max_{|v|=m_u}\sup_{x\ne x'}\frac{|D^v g(x)-D^v g(x')|}{\lVert x-x'\rVert_2^{u-m_u}}\le L\right\},\qquad m_u=\lceil u\rceil-1.\]

definitions.name: \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{band},n}
definitions.construction: \[\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{band},n}(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,d,L,\varepsilon,f_{-},f_{+},x_0)=\left\{P:\text{for this }n\in\mathbb{N},\text{ every member property enumerated below holds}\right\}.\]

definitions.name: R_n^{\mathrm{band}}
definitions.construction: \[R_n^{\mathrm{band}}=\inf_{T_n}\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{band},n}}\mathbb{E}_P\left|T_n(O_{1:n})-\tau_P(x_0)\right|,\] where the infimum is over all measurable estimators \(T_n\).

definitions.name: \widehat{\tau}^{\mathrm{cap}}_n(x_0)
definitions.construction:
For \(n\geq3\), partition the indices deterministically into three folds \(I_1,I_2,I_3\) whose sizes differ by at most one, and use the three cyclic choices \((I_{r},I_{r+1},I_{r+2})\) as two nuisance folds and one evaluation fold.  For \(v\in\{\alpha,\beta\}\), let \(\mathcal B_{v,n}\) be the Lebesgue-orthonormal basis obtained by partitioning \([0,1]^d\) into the largest regular tensor grid for which the cellwise tensor polynomials of total degree \(\lceil v\rceil-1\) have total dimension at most \(k_n\).  On \(I_r\), estimate \(\pi_P\) by least squares of \(A\) on \(\mathcal B_{\alpha,n}\); on the independent fold \(I_{r+1}\), estimate a second copy of \(\pi_P\) in the same way and estimate \(\eta_P(x)=\mathbb E_P[Y\mid X=x]\) by least squares of \(Y\) on \(\mathcal B_{\beta,n}\).  In each nuisance least-squares fit, replace the empirical Gram matrix \(G=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_j)U^\top\) by
\[
\mathsf C_{\mathrm{nuis}}(G)=U\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\min\{2f_+,\max\{f_-/2,\lambda_j\}\}\right)U^\top.
\]
Clip the two propensity predictions to \([\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]\) and the outcome prediction to \([-1,1]\); denote them by \(\widehat\pi_{r,a}\), \(\widehat\pi_{r,b}\), and \(\widehat\eta_r\).

Let \(\mathcal C=[-1/2,1/2]^d\), let \(b_\gamma\) be the vector of Lebesgue-orthonormal polynomials on \(\mathcal C\) of total degree at most \(\lceil\gamma\rceil-1\), and put \(b_{i,h}=b_\gamma((X_i-x_0)/h_n)\) and \(K_{i,h}=h_n^{-d}\mathbf1\{(X_i-x_0)/h_n\in\mathcal C\}\).  On \(I_{r+2}\), form
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat Q_r&=\frac1{|I_{r+2}|}\sum_{i\in I_{r+2}}K_{i,h}b_{i,h}b_{i,h}^\top
\{A_i-\widehat\pi_{r,a}(X_i)\}\{A_i-\widehat\pi_{r,b}(X_i)\},\\
\widehat S_r&=\frac1{|I_{r+2}|}\sum_{i\in I_{r+2}}K_{i,h}b_{i,h}
\{A_i-\widehat\pi_{r,a}(X_i)\}\{Y_i-\widehat\eta_r(X_i)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Define \(\mathsf C_{\mathrm{loc}}\) by spectral clipping to
\([\varepsilon^2f_-/2,2f_+]\), put
\(\widehat\theta_r=\mathsf C_{\mathrm{loc}}(\widehat Q_r)^{-1}\widehat S_r\),
and take the fold estimate \(b_\gamma(0)^\top\widehat\theta_r\).  The estimator
\(\widehat\tau_n^{\mathrm{cap}}(x_0)\) is the truncation to \([-2,2]\) of the average of the three cyclic fold estimates.  For \(n<3\), define it to be zero.  Spectral clipping is the matrix functional in the displays and is independent of the choice of eigenvectors, so this construction specifies a measurable value on singular matrices and eigenvalue ties.

definitions.name: \mathfrak{H}^{\mathrm{dens}}_n
definitions.construction: Begin from a density strictly inside \([f_{-},f_{+}]\). Partition a shrinking cube around \(x_0\) into paired cells, place mean-zero signed wavelet perturbations in \(f_P\), and couple their signs with flat-top perturbations of \(\pi_P\) and \(\mu_{a,P}\). Mix independently over the paired signs and choose cell width and amplitude by the H\"older constraints and the Hellinger distance between the two \(n\)-fold mixtures. This program is denoted by \(\mathfrak{H}^{\mathrm{dens}}_n\).

definitions.name: \mathfrak{H}^{\mathrm{asym}}
definitions.construction: Combine same-sample M\"obius-stabilized Gram corrections with two resolution levels, one adapted to \(\pi_P\) and one adapted to \(\mu_{a,P}\), and pair the estimator analysis with unequal-resolution mean-zero density perturbations inside the fixed density band. The resulting estimator-and-testing program is denoted by \(\mathfrak{H}^{\mathrm{asym}}\).

statements.statement: For every \(P\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{band},n}\), the continuous versions selected by the H\"older restrictions satisfy \[\tau_P(x_0)=\mathbb{E}_P[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x_0].\]
statements.justification: This selects a law-functional version of the point target before any minimax comparison is made.
statements.gap: The downgraded prior CausalSmith proposal left the unrestricted conditional mean at \(x_0\) version-dependent; the H\"older class used by Kennedy et al. selects a continuous version.
statements.consumer: The minimax risk \(R_n^{\mathrm{band}}\) and every downstream estimator comparison use this identified point target.
statements.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{band},n}\).  For \(a\in\{0,1\}\), let
\(g_a(X)\) be an arbitrary regular version of
\(\mathbb E_P[Y(a)\mid X]\), and put \(e_1=\pi_P\) and
\(e_0=1-\pi_P\).  If \(\varphi\) is bounded and measurable, consistency gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_P[\varphi(X)\mathbf 1\{A=a\}Y]
&=\mathbb E_P[\varphi(X)\mathbf 1\{A=a\}Y(a)] .
\end{aligned}
\]
Conditional exchangeability and iterated expectation then give
\[
\mathbb E_P[\varphi(X)\mathbf 1\{A=a\}Y(a)]
=\mathbb E_P[\varphi(X)e_a(X)g_a(X)].
\]
On the other hand, the definition of \(\mu_{a,P}\) gives
\[
\mathbb E_P[\varphi(X)\mathbf 1\{A=a\}Y]
=\mathbb E_P[\varphi(X)e_a(X)\mu_{a,P}(X)].
\]
Because these identities hold for every \(\varphi\),
\(e_a(g_a-\mu_{a,P})=0\) \(P_X\)-almost surely.  Uniform overlap gives
\(e_a\geq\varepsilon>0\), so
\[
g_a=\mu_{a,P}\qquad P_X\text{-almost surely}.
\]
Consequently \(\mu_{1,P}-\mu_{0,P}=\tau_P\) is a version of
\(\mathbb E_P[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X]\).  The H\"older restrictions provide a
continuous version of \(\tau_P\).  Equivalently, one may select the two
potential-outcome conditional-mean versions to be
\(g_a^{\mathrm c}=\mu_{a,P}\), whose difference is that same continuous
version.  Since \(x_0\) is an interior point and the displayed conditional
expectation is, as the statement says, evaluated in this selected continuous
version, evaluation yields
\[
\tau_P(x_0)=\mathbb E_P[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x_0].
\]

statements.statement: Fix \(d,L,\varepsilon,f_{-},f_{+},x_0\). Uniformly over compact subsets of \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{low}}\), there are constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\) such that for every \(n\ge n_0\), \[R_n^{\mathrm{band}}\ge c\,r_n^{\mathrm{band}}.\] In particular, the \(n^{-(\alpha+\beta)/d}\) branch is generated by alternatives from \(\mathfrak{H}^{\mathrm{dens}}_n\) whose covariate densities remain normalized and inside the same fixed two-sided band.
statements.justification: This is the new information bound showing that an unsmooth observed design law can be first-order for a localized causal functional.
statements.gap: Kennedy et al. (2024, Theorem 1 and the following density remark) obtain the faster localized fuzzy-hypothesis lower bound but use a design with holes; no published converse couples density perturbations to the causal nuisances while retaining a fixed positive lower density bound.
statements.consumer: It determines when no density-free pointwise CATE procedure can inherit the known-density KBRW benchmark.

statements.statement: Fix \(d,L,\varepsilon,f_{-},f_{+},x_0\). Uniformly over compact subsets of \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{low}}\), there are constants \(C<\infty\) and \(n_0\) such that for every \(n\ge n_0\), \[\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{band},n}}\mathbb{E}_P\left|\widehat{\tau}^{\mathrm{cap}}_n(x_0)-\tau_P(x_0)\right|\le C\,\overline r_n^{\mathrm{band}}.\]
statements.justification: A primitive-class upper bound turns the density lower bound into a frontier rather than an isolated impossibility witness.
statements.gap: Kennedy (2023, Corollary 3) gives the same polynomial exponent only under high-level linear-smoother and Gram conditions; this theorem derives those conditions uniformly from the fixed density band and gives an explicit feasible construction.
statements.consumer: It supplies a rate-certified procedure for pointwise treatment-effect heterogeneity when estimating a smooth multivariate design density is indefensible.

statements.statement: Under the preceding conditions, uniformly over compact subsets of \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{low}}\), \[r_n^{\mathrm{band}}\lesssim R_n^{\mathrm{band}}\lesssim\overline r_n^{\mathrm{band}}.\] Consequently, \(R_n^{\mathrm{band}}\) has polynomial minimax exponent \((\alpha+\beta)/d\) throughout \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{low}}\), up to the displayed logarithmic factor.
statements.justification: The matched polynomial exponent identifies the design density as a first-order component of the CATE minimax problem.
statements.gap: Kennedy et al. (2024) leave the lower-bound and upper-bound density scopes unmatched, while Kennedy (2023) supplies only an estimator-side exponent; the theorem closes both directions over one primitive band-only class.
statements.consumer: It converts the earlier rate \(n^{-(\alpha+\beta)/d}\) from a method-specific guarantee into the correct polynomial benchmark for method comparison.

statements.statement: For every \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{low}}\), \[\frac{R_n^{\mathrm{band}}}{r_n^{\mathrm{KBRW}}}\longrightarrow\infty.\] More precisely, the lower bound contains the polynomial factor \(n^{1/(1+d/(2\gamma)+d/(4s))-(\alpha+\beta)/d}\), whose exponent is strictly positive on \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{low}}\).
statements.justification: This states the strict open-region comparison required to distinguish a genuine density bottleneck from a technical condition in one estimator.
statements.gap: Kennedy et al. (2024, Remark 8) suspect density dependence but do not exhibit a region with polynomial separation from their benchmark.
statements.consumer: It tells users of localized higher-order CATE estimators exactly when the published KBRW benchmark is unattainable without design regularity.

statements.statement: If \(\pi_P\) and both \(\mu_{a,P}\) are supplied as functions, then the direct plug-in \(\mu_{1,P}(x_0)-\mu_{0,P}(x_0)\) equals \(\tau_P(x_0)\) and has zero error.  Separately, oracleize the corrected weighted local \(R\)-normal equations defining \(\widehat{\tau}^{\mathrm{cap}}_n(x_0)\) by replacing their two propensity fits by \(\pi_P\) and their outcome fit by \(\eta_P=\pi_P\mu_{1,P}+(1-\pi_P)\mu_{0,P}\), while retaining the evaluation sample, local-polynomial stage, spectral safeguard, and truncation.  The resulting oracleized estimator has conditional target \(\tau_P\) and, uniformly under the preceding conditions, mean-absolute error \(O(n^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)})\).
statements.proof_tex:
The direct plug-in assertion follows immediately from the defining identity
\[
\tau_P(x_0)=\mu_{1,P}(x_0)-\mu_{0,P}(x_0).
\]
We prove the nontrivial assertion about the oracleized sample estimator.  Put
\[
\eta_P(x)=\pi_P(x)\mu_{1,P}(x)+(1-\pi_P(x))\mu_{0,P}(x),\qquad
\nu_P(x)=\pi_P(x)\{1-\pi_P(x)\}.
\]
For the oracleized normal equations, define
\[
Z_P=\frac{Y-\eta_P(X)}{A-\pi_P(X)},\qquad
W_P=\{A-\pi_P(X)\}^2.
\]
The denominator is bounded away from zero because \(A\in\{0,1\}\) and
\(\varepsilon\leq\pi_P\leq1-\varepsilon\); bounded outcomes give
\(|Z_P|\leq2/\varepsilon\).  Moreover,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_P[W_PZ_P\mid X]
&=\mathbb E_P[(A-\pi_P(X))(Y-\eta_P(X))\mid X]\\
&=\pi_P(X)\{1-\pi_P(X)\}\{\mu_{1,P}(X)-\mu_{0,P}(X)\}\\
&=\nu_P(X)\tau_P(X),\\
\mathbb E_P[W_P\mid X]&=\nu_P(X).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the weighted conditional regression function of \(Z_P\) is exactly
\(\tau_P\), not a newly defined estimand.

With \(h_n=n^{-1/(2\gamma+d)}\), the oracleized evaluation equations are
weighted local-polynomial normal equations for this regression, with the
monomial vector through degree \(\lceil\gamma\rceil-1\).  Their population
local Gram matrix is an integral against
\(\nu_P(x)f_P(x)\).  Density-band and overlap bounds give
\[
\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)f_-\leq
\nu_P(x)f_P(x)\leq f_+/4,
\]
so its eigenvalues are bounded above and below by positive constants depending
only on the fixed polynomial moment matrix and the displayed class constants.
The spectral safeguard in the corrected construction is therefore inactive
whenever the empirical Gram differs from its expectation by less than half
the population lower eigenvalue.  A direct independence and second-moment
calculation, entry by entry in the fixed-dimensional Gram matrix, bounds the
probability of the complementary event by \(C/(nh_n^d)\).

On the good-Gram event, the Taylor polynomial of \(\tau_P\) at \(x_0\) has
uniform remainder at most \(CLh_n^\gamma\).  Substitution in the weighted
normal equations therefore bounds the deterministic approximation part of
the fitted intercept by \(Ch_n^\gamma\).  Conditional on the design and
treatments, the centered summands
\[
W_P\{Z_P-\tau_P(X)\}
\]
are uniformly bounded and have conditional mean zero after averaging over
treatment and outcome at each covariate.  The local Gram bounds then give
variance at most \(C/(nh_n^d)\) for the fitted intercept.  Jensen's inequality
turns this into mean absolute noise at most \(C(nh_n^d)^{-1/2}\).  Truncation
to \([-2,2]\) cannot increase error and makes the bad-Gram contribution at
most \(C/(nh_n^d)\).  Hence
\[
\mathbb E_P|\widehat\tau_n^{\mathrm{or}}(x_0)-\tau_P(x_0)|
\leq C\left\{h_n^\gamma+(nh_n^d)^{-1/2}+(nh_n^d)^{-1}\right\}
\leq Cn^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}.
\]
The calculation uses only the fixed density band, overlap, bounded outcomes,
H\"older CATE condition, and independent sampling, so the constant is uniform
over the stated class and compact smoothness subsets.
statements.justification: The reduction is the required sanity check that the new frontier retains the classical oracle regression branch.
statements.gap: The new density-coupled argument must not manufacture a slowdown when the causal nuisances are supplied; this reduction pins down that boundary case.
statements.consumer: It lets local-polynomial CATE theory and software recover the standard random-design regression rate as a direct special case.

statements.statement: Using \(\mathfrak{H}^{\mathrm{asym}}\), determine whether the logarithmic factor in the upper bound can be removed and characterize the exact minimax rate over the remaining low-smoothness parameter orderings, including \(\alpha<\beta\), without imposing any regularity on \(f_P\) beyond \(f_{-}\le f_P\le f_{+}\).
statements.justification: The exact constant-order frontier and asymmetric smoothness regimes are the genuinely unresolved content beyond the polynomial slowdown theorem.
statements.gap: Neither Kennedy (2023) nor Kennedy et al. (2024) treats the band-only asymmetric frontier, and the empirical-HOIF papers do not permit projection dimension beyond sample rank.
statements.consumer: A resolution would determine whether one tuning rule is minimax across both nuisance orderings or whether distinct density bottlenecks arise.

statements.statement:
The set \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{low}}\) is nonempty.  Moreover, for every
\((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\in\mathcal R_{\mathrm{low}}\), if
\[
p=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{d}=\frac{2s}{d},\qquad
t=\frac{1}{1+d/(2\gamma)+d/(4s)},\qquad
q=\frac{\gamma}{2\gamma+d},
\]
then \(0<p<t<q<1/2\).
statements.proof_tex:
For nonemptiness, take
\((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(d/8,d/16,d)\).  Then
\(\beta<\min(\alpha,\gamma)\), \(s=3d/32\), and
\[
\frac{3d}{32}<\frac{d/4}{1+d/(2d)}=\frac d6,
\]
so this triple belongs to \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{low}}\).

Now fix any member of the region.  Its strict smoothness inequality is
\[
s<\frac{d/4}{1+d/(2\gamma)}.
\]
Multiplication by the positive denominators shows that this is equivalent to
\[
\frac{2s}{d}+\frac{s}{\gamma}<\frac12. \tag{1}
\]
Since \(p=2s/d\), a direct calculation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
t>p
&\Longleftrightarrow
d>2s\left(1+\frac d{2\gamma}+\frac d{4s}\right)\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\frac{2s}{d}+\frac{s}{\gamma}<\frac12,
\end{aligned}
\]
which is (1).  The defining inequality also gives
\[
\frac d{4s}>1+\frac d{2\gamma}.
\]
Therefore
\[
1+\frac d{2\gamma}+\frac d{4s}>2+\frac d\gamma,
\]
and taking positive reciprocals gives
\(t<(2+d/\gamma)^{-1}=q\).  Finally \(p>0\) and
\(q=\gamma/(2\gamma+d)<1/2\), completing the chain.

statements.statement:
Fix \(d,L,\varepsilon,f_-,f_+\), and \(x_0\).  Uniformly over compact
subsets of \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{low}}\), there are constants \(c>0\) and
\(n_0\) such that, for every \(n\geq n_0\),
\[
R_n^{\mathrm{band}}\geq c\,n^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}.
\]
statements.proof_tex:
Let \(K\) be a compact subset of \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{low}}\).  Choose a
nonnegative \(C^\infty\) function \(\psi\), supported on
\(\{z:\lVert z\rVert_\infty\leq1/2\}\), with \(\psi(0)=1\).  For a constant
\(c_*>0\) to be chosen, put
\[
H=n^{-1/(2\gamma+d)},\qquad
\delta=c_*H^\gamma,\qquad
\tau_1(x)=\delta\,\psi\!\left(\frac{x-x_0}{H}\right),\qquad
\tau_0(x)=0.
\]
Compactness of \(K\) and interiority of \(x_0\) give a common \(n_0\) for
which the support of the bump is contained in \([0,1]^d\).  The scaled-bump
calculation in the definition of the H\"older ball gives, uniformly over
\(K\),
\[
\lVert\tau_1\rVert_{\mathcal H^\gamma_d}\leq C_Kc_*.
\]
Furthermore \(\beta<\gamma\) on \(K\), with the gap bounded away from zero,
so
\[
\left\lVert\frac{\tau_1}{2}\right\rVert_{\mathcal H^\beta_d}
\leq C_Kc_*H^{\gamma-\beta}\leq C_Kc_*.
\]
Choose \(c_*\) small enough that these norms are at most \(L\) and all means
below lie in \([-1/2,1/2]\).

We now construct two full-data laws.  Under both, \(X\) is uniform on
\([0,1]^d\), \(A\mid X\) is Bernoulli with probability \(1/2\), and \(A\) is
conditionally independent of the potential outcomes.  Under \(P_j\), set
\[
\mu_{1,j}(x)=\frac{\tau_j(x)}2,\qquad
\mu_{0,j}(x)=-\frac{\tau_j(x)}2,\qquad j\in\{0,1\},
\]
and, conditionally on \(X=x\), let \(Y(a)\in\{-1,1\}\) have mean
\(\mu_{a,j}(x)\); the two potential outcomes may be taken conditionally
independent.  Finally define \(Y=AY(1)+(1-A)Y(0)\).  Thus consistency and
conditional exchangeability hold by construction.  The propensity is the
constant \(1/2\), so overlap and every propensity H\"older condition hold.
The preceding scaled-bump bounds give the outcome-regression and CATE
H\"older conditions.  The potential outcomes are bounded, and the uniform
density is normalized and satisfies \(f_-<1<f_+\).  Hence \(P_0,P_1\) both
belong to \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{band},n}\).

It remains to bound their statistical distance without invoking an
unproved testing result.  Use the convention
\(H^2(Q_1,Q_0)=\int(\sqrt{q_1}-\sqrt{q_0})^2\).  Conditional on \(X=x\) and
\(A=a\), the outcome is a Rademacher variable whose mean changes from zero
to \(m_a(x)\), where \(|m_a(x)|=|\tau_1(x)|/2\).  Its chi-square divergence
from the mean-zero Rademacher law equals \(m_a(x)^2\), and squared Hellinger
distance is no larger than chi-square divergence.  Averaging over \(X,A\)
therefore yields
\[
H^2(P_{1,O},P_{0,O})\leq C\int\tau_1(x)^2\,dx
\leq C_K\delta^2H^d.
\]
Hellinger affinity tensorizes, so the identity
\[
H^2(P_{1,O}^{\otimes n},P_{0,O}^{\otimes n})
=2-2\left(1-\frac{H^2(P_{1,O},P_{0,O})}{2}\right)^n
\]
and \(1-(1-z)^n\leq nz\) imply
\[
H^2(P_{1,O}^{\otimes n},P_{0,O}^{\otimes n})
\leq C_Kn\delta^2H^d=C_Kc_*^2.
\]
Choose \(c_*\) still smaller so that the last Hellinger distance is at most
\(1/2\).  Cauchy--Schwarz applied to
\(|p-q|=|\sqrt p-\sqrt q|(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)\) gives total variation no larger
than Hellinger distance, hence at most \(1/2\).

For any estimator \(T_n\), the point targets are separated by
\(\tau_1(x_0)-\tau_0(x_0)=\delta\).  Pointwise, the triangle inequality gives
\(|T_n-\tau_0(x_0)|+|T_n-\tau_1(x_0)|\geq\delta\).  Integrating this inequality
against the minimum of the two \(n\)-sample densities yields
\[
\max_{j\in\{0,1\}}\mathbb E_{P_j}|T_n-\tau_j(x_0)|
\geq\frac{\delta}{2}\{1-\operatorname{TV}(P_{1,O}^{\otimes n},P_{0,O}^{\otimes n})\}
\geq\frac{\delta}{4}.
\]
Taking the infimum over \(T_n\) proves the result because
\(\delta=c_*n^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}\).  All constants were chosen uniformly
over \(K\).

statements.statement:
Fix \(d,L,\varepsilon,f_-,f_+\), and \(x_0\).  Uniformly over compact
subsets of \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{low}}\), there are constants \(C<\infty\)
and \(n_0\) such that, for every \(n\geq n_0\),
\[
R_n^{\mathrm{band}}\leq C\,n^{-\beta/(2\beta+d)}.
\]
statements.proof_tex:
We give one data-driven estimator and bound its risk.  Let \(K\) be a compact
subset of \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{low}}\), put
\(\ell=n^{-1/(2\beta+d)}\), and let
\(v_\beta(z)\) be the vector of monomials \(z^r\) with
\(|r|\leq\lceil\beta\rceil-1\).  Write
\(\mathcal C=[-1/2,1/2]^d\) and
\[
M_\beta=\int_{\mathcal C}v_\beta(z)v_\beta(z)^\top\,dz.
\]
This is a fixed positive-definite matrix.  For \(a\in\{0,1\}\), define
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat Q_a
&=\frac1{n\ell^d}\sum_{i=1}^n
\mathbf1\{A_i=a\}\mathbf1\{(X_i-x_0)/\ell\in\mathcal C\}
v_\beta((X_i-x_0)/\ell)v_\beta((X_i-x_0)/\ell)^\top,\\
\widehat S_a
&=\frac1{n\ell^d}\sum_{i=1}^n
\mathbf1\{A_i=a\}\mathbf1\{(X_i-x_0)/\ell\in\mathcal C\}
v_\beta((X_i-x_0)/\ell)Y_i.
\end{aligned}
\]
Let \(\mathsf C_a(\widehat Q_a)\) denote spectral clipping of
\(\widehat Q_a\) to
\[
\left[\frac{\varepsilon f_-\lambda_{\min}(M_\beta)}2,
2f_+\lambda_{\max}(M_\beta)\right].
\]
Define
\[
\widehat\mu_a(x_0)=\operatorname{clip}_{[-1,1]}\!\left\{
v_\beta(0)^\top\mathsf C_a(\widehat Q_a)^{-1}\widehat S_a\right\},\qquad
T_n=\operatorname{clip}_{[-2,2]}\{\widehat\mu_1(x_0)-\widehat\mu_0(x_0)\}.
\]
This is an explicit measurable estimator, including on singular empirical
designs.

For all sufficiently large \(n\), the localization cube is contained in the
support.  If \(e_1=\pi_P\) and \(e_0=1-\pi_P\), change of variables gives
\[
\mathbb E_P\widehat Q_a
=\int_{\mathcal C}e_a(x_0+\ell z)f_P(x_0+\ell z)
v_\beta(z)v_\beta(z)^\top\,dz.
\]
The density band and overlap imply
\[
\varepsilon f_-M_\beta\preceq\mathbb E_P\widehat Q_a\preceq f_+M_\beta.
\tag{2}
\]
The dimension of \(v_\beta\) is bounded uniformly on \(K\), and its entries
are bounded on \(\mathcal C\).  Independence and a direct second-moment
calculation consequently give
\[
\mathbb E_P\lVert\widehat Q_a-\mathbb E_P\widehat Q_a\rVert_F^2
\leq\frac{C_K}{n\ell^d}.
\]
Markov's inequality and (2) show that the probability that spectral clipping
is active is at most \(C_K/(n\ell^d)\).

On the complementary event, take the Taylor polynomial of
\(\mu_{a,P}\) at \(x_0\) through degree \(\lceil\beta\rceil-1\).  The defining
H\"older inequality, including the integer-order boundary case, gives
\[
\mu_{a,P}(x_0+\ell z)=v_\beta(z)^\top\theta_a+r_a(z),\qquad
\sup_{z\in\mathcal C}|r_a(z)|\leq C_KL\ell^\beta.
\]
Substitution in the normal equations decomposes the coefficient error into
a remainder part and a centered outcome-noise part.  Bound (2), the good
event, and the constant coordinate of \(v_\beta\) bound the remainder part
by \(C_K\ell^\beta\).  Conditional on \(X_{1:n},A_{1:n}\), bounded outcomes
and the same Gram bounds give variance at most \(C_K/(n\ell^d)\) for the
fitted intercept.  Jensen's inequality therefore gives conditional mean
absolute noise at most \(C_K(n\ell^d)^{-1/2}\).  Truncation cannot increase
error because \(\mu_{a,P}(x_0)\in[-1,1]\); on the bad-Gram event it bounds
the error by \(2\).  Thus
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{band},n}}
\mathbb E_P|\widehat\mu_a(x_0)-\mu_{a,P}(x_0)|
\leq C_K\left\{\ell^\beta+(n\ell^d)^{-1/2}+(n\ell^d)^{-1}\right\}.
\]
The final term is no larger than the middle term for large \(n\).  Applying
the triangle inequality to the two arms and using
\(\ell=n^{-1/(2\beta+d)}\) yields
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{band},n}}
\mathbb E_P|T_n-\tau_P(x_0)|\leq C_Kn^{-\beta/(2\beta+d)}.
\]
The minimax upper bound follows by using this single \(T_n\) in the
infimum defining \(R_n^{\mathrm{band}}\).

sampling_model.design: An i.i.d. observational random-design experiment with an unknown Lebesgue density satisfying only \(f_{-}\le f_P\le f_{+}\).
sampling_model.units: Each unit contributes \(O=(Y,A,X)\), with \(X\in[0,1]^d\) and bounded potential outcomes.
sampling_model.treatment: Treatment is binary and conditionally exchangeable given \(X\).
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: Cross-fitted partition-series regressions are capped at dimension \(k_n=\lfloor n/(\log n)^2\rfloor\); no estimator of \(f_P\) and no density modulus are used.

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: The pointwise CATE lower bound permits a merely bounded design density, while attainment of the displayed rate requires additional control of the localized covariate law.

The undersmoothed local-polynomial R-learner has pointwise error of polynomial order \(n^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}\vee n^{-(\alpha+\beta)/d}\), and minimax optimality of the non-oracle branch is left open.
Empirical inverse-Gram HOIF estimators remove density smoothness for global average functionals when projection dimension is smaller than sample size.
Same-sample stabilization gives global bilinear-form guarantees for \(k=o(n)\) and leaves \(k\gtrsim n\) to future work.
A random-design U-statistic and local-polynomial construction attains a regression-functional minimax frontier without smoothness of the design density.

tldr: The proposal establishes that an unknown covariate density confined only to a fixed positive band is a first-order nuisance for pointwise CATE estimation. A density-coupled fuzzy-hypothesis lower bound and a rank-capped local R-learner bracket the minimax mean-absolute risk at polynomial order \(n^{-(\alpha+\beta)/d}\) on a nonempty open low-smoothness region. This rate is polynomially slower than the Kennedy--Balakrishnan--Robins--Wasserman benchmark, explaining why global empirical HOIF density removal does not survive pointwise localization when the required projection dimension exceeds the available design rank.

project_justification.gap: Kennedy et al. prove their pointwise CATE lower bound over a broad bounded-density model but attain the displayed rate only with additional covariate-law control; their paper explicitly leaves the role of the density unresolved. Global empirical and stabilized HOIF papers eliminate density smoothness only while projection dimension remains below sample rank.
project_justification.niche: In the low-smoothness CATE regime, the localized KBRW bias balance calls for more nuisance resolution than a band-only random design can empirically support. This creates a testable rate separation rather than a generic complaint about density estimation.
project_justification.fill: The project constructs normalized, two-sided-banded density perturbations coupled to the propensity and outcome regressions, proves the resulting \(n^{-(\alpha+\beta)/d}\) lower branch, and matches its polynomial exponent with a feasible rank-capped local R-learner.

related_work: Kennedy, Balakrishnan, Robins, and Wasserman (2024, Theorem 1, Remark 8, and the Discussion) provide the writing model and the exact localized fuzzy-hypothesis benchmark; the present result sharpens their explicit density-scope question by proving a strict open-region separation. Kennedy (2023, Corollary 3 and the subsection on faster rates with known covariate density) provides the estimator-side \(n^{-(\alpha+\beta)/d}\) branch; the present lower bound turns that method-specific rate into a polynomial minimax frontier over a primitive band-only class. Liu, Mukherjee, Newey, and Robins (2017, Theorem 2 and the Discussion) motivate empirical Gram replacement but restrict projection dimension below sample size. Liu, Li, Gu, and Liu (2026, Theorem 1 and Concluding Remark 1) supply the same-sample stabilization and explicitly leave \(k\gtrsim n\) open; their graph-counting method informs the unresolved log-free extension rather than serving as a theorem-level target. Shen, Gao, Witten, and Han (2020, Sections 2--3) show how random-design U-statistics and paired perturbations can avoid density smoothness in a different regression-functional problem. Robins et al. (2016) give changing-kernel quadratic limit theory relevant to later inference but do not determine the pointwise CATE minimax rate.
technical_internal_limitation: The KBRW optimal localized projection dimension exceeds the local effective sample size throughout the strict low-smoothness region, but rank deficiency alone is not an information lower bound. The load-bearing theorem must establish mixture indistinguishability after joint density and causal-nuisance perturbation; it cannot argue from failure of an empirical Gram estimator.
honest_scope: The core claims a matched polynomial exponent and a polynomial separation from \(r_n^{\mathrm{KBRW}}\), with an explicit logarithmic gap in the upper bound. Exact constant-order minimaxity, removal of the log factor, and the ordering \(\alpha<\beta\) remain in \(\mathrm{oeq:exact-asymmetric-frontier}\). If the nuisances are known, the construction reduces to the classical pointwise regression rate.
